title: Implement a Stack class
intro: A stack stores items in a list with LIFO (last in, first out) behaviour. Build the class part by part: constructor, push, then pop. Run the tests after each part to check your code. (2025 P2 data structures.)

parts.instruction: Write the constructor __init__ that stores the items in a list attribute self._items, and is_empty() which returns True when the stack holds nothing.
parts.tests:
s = Stack()
assert s.is_empty() == True, 'a new stack should be empty'
s._items.append(1)
assert s.is_empty() == False, 'a stack with an item is not empty'

parts.instruction: Add push(item), which puts item on top of the stack.
parts.tests:
s = Stack()
s.push(7)
s.push(9)
assert s.is_empty() == False, 'push should add an item'
assert s._items == [7, 9], 'push should put the item on top (end of the list)'
parts.model:
def push(self, item):
        self._items.append(item)

parts.instruction: Add pop(), which removes and returns the top item. If the stack is empty, return None instead of crashing.
parts.tests:
s = Stack()
assert s.pop() is None, 'pop on an empty stack should return None'
s.push(4)
s.push(6)
assert s.pop() == 6, 'pop should return the top item'
assert s.pop() == 4, 'pop returns items in LIFO order'
assert s.is_empty() == True, 'the stack should be empty after popping everything'

title: Implement a linked list
intro: A linear linked list chains nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next node. Build it part by part: nodes and the constructor, insertion and traversal, then search and delete. (Syllabus 1.3.5 / 2.3.3: create, insert, delete and search for a linear linked list.)

parts.instruction: Write a Node class whose constructor stores data in self.data and sets self.next to None. Then write the LinkedList constructor with self.head set to None, and is_empty() which returns True when the list holds nothing.
parts.tests:
ll = LinkedList()
assert ll.is_empty() == True, 'a new list should be empty'
n = Node(5)
assert n.data == 5 and n.next is None, 'a node stores data and starts with next = None'

parts.instruction: Add insert_at_front(data), which puts a new node at the head of the list, and to_list(), which walks the chain and returns the data as a Python list, head first.
parts.tests:
ll = LinkedList()
ll.insert_at_front(3)
ll.insert_at_front(1)
ll.insert_at_front(4)
assert ll.is_empty() == False, 'the list should not be empty after inserts'
assert ll.to_list() == [4, 1, 3], 'the newest node should be at the head'
parts.model:
def insert_at_front(self, data):
        node = Node(data)
        node.next = self.head
        self.head = node

    def to_list(self):
        out = []
        cur = self.head
        while cur is not None:
            out.append(cur.data)
            cur = cur.next
        return out

parts.instruction: Add find(target), which returns True if any node holds target, and delete(target), which removes the FIRST node holding target and returns True, or returns False if target is not in the list. delete must work for the head node, the last node and an empty list.
parts.tests:
ll = LinkedList()
assert ll.find(1) == False and ll.delete(1) == False, 'an empty list holds nothing'
for x in [3, 1, 4, 1]:
    ll.insert_at_front(x)
assert ll.to_list() == [1, 4, 1, 3]
assert ll.find(4) == True and ll.find(9) == False, 'find walks the chain'
assert ll.delete(1) == True and ll.to_list() == [4, 1, 3], 'delete removes the first matching node (the head here)'
assert ll.delete(3) == True and ll.to_list() == [4, 1], 'delete unlinks the last node too'
assert ll.delete(9) == False and ll.to_list() == [4, 1], 'deleting a missing value changes nothing'

title: Implement a circular queue
intro: A circular queue stores items in a fixed-size list and wraps the front and rear indexes around when they reach the end, so freed slots get reused. Build it part by part: constructor and state checks, enqueue, then dequeue. (Syllabus 1.3.3 / 2.3.3: create, insert and delete for linear and circular queues.)

parts.instruction: Write the constructor __init__(capacity) that sets up a fixed-size list self._items of capacity None values, plus self._capacity, self._front, self._rear and a count self._count. Then write is_empty() and is_full() using the count.
parts.tests:
q = CircularQueue(3)
assert q.is_empty() == True and q.is_full() == False, 'a new queue is empty, not full'
assert len(q._items) == 3, 'the underlying list has exactly capacity slots'

parts.instruction: Add enqueue(item). It returns False when the queue is full. Otherwise it moves _rear forward by one slot, wrapping back to index 0 at the end of the list, stores the item there, and returns True. (Wrap with modulo: (self._rear + 1) % self._capacity.)
parts.tests:
q = CircularQueue(3)
assert q.enqueue('a') == True and q.enqueue('b') == True and q.enqueue('c') == True
assert q.is_full() == True, 'three items fill a capacity-3 queue'
assert q.enqueue('d') == False, 'enqueue on a full queue returns False'
assert q._rear == 2, 'rear sits on the last stored item'
parts.model:
def enqueue(self, item):
        if self.is_full():
            return False
        self._rear = (self._rear + 1) % self._capacity
        self._items[self._rear] = item
        self._count += 1
        return True

parts.instruction: Add dequeue(). It returns None when the queue is empty. Otherwise it returns the item at _front and moves _front forward, wrapping around. After some dequeues, enqueue must reuse the freed slots - that is what makes the queue circular.
parts.tests:
q = CircularQueue(3)
assert q.dequeue() is None, 'dequeue on an empty queue returns None'
q.enqueue('a'); q.enqueue('b'); q.enqueue('c')
assert q.dequeue() == 'a' and q.dequeue() == 'b', 'items leave in FIFO order'
assert q.enqueue('d') == True and q.enqueue('e') == True, 'freed slots get reused'
assert q.dequeue() == 'c' and q.dequeue() == 'd' and q.dequeue() == 'e', 'order stays FIFO after wrapping'
assert q.is_empty() == True, 'the queue is empty again at the end'
parts.model:
def dequeue(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            return None
        item = self._items[self._front]
        self._front = (self._front + 1) % self._capacity
        self._count -= 1
        return item

title: Implement a binary search tree (no delete)
intro: A binary search tree keeps smaller values in the left subtree and larger values in the right subtree, so search only walks one path down. Build it part by part: insert, search, then an in-order traversal that returns the values sorted. The 2026 syllabus excludes deleting BST nodes, so this practical stops at insert, search and traverse. (Syllabus 1.3.6-1.3.7 / 2.3.3.)

parts.instruction: Write a Node class holding self.data, self.left and self.right. Then write the BST constructor with self.root = None, and insert(data), which walks left or right from the root until it finds the empty spot where data belongs and attaches a new node there. If data is already in the tree, do nothing.
parts.tests:
t = BST()
t.insert(5)
assert t.root.data == 5, 'the first insert becomes the root'
t.insert(3)
t.insert(8)
assert t.root.left.data == 3 and t.root.right.data == 8, 'smaller goes left, larger goes right'
t.insert(8)
assert t.root.right.left is None and t.root.right.right is None, 'inserting a duplicate changes nothing'

parts.instruction: Add search(data), which returns True if data is in the tree and False otherwise. Follow the same left/right rule as insert instead of visiting every node.
parts.tests:
t = BST()
for x in [5, 3, 8, 1, 4]:
    t.insert(x)
assert t.search(4) == True and t.search(1) == True, 'search finds stored values'
assert t.search(7) == False and t.search(0) == False, 'search returns False for missing values'
assert BST().search(1) == False, 'an empty tree holds nothing'

parts.instruction: Add inorder(), which returns the values as a Python list using in-order traversal (left subtree, node, right subtree). For a BST this visits the values in sorted order - the classic application of in-order traversal. Use an inner recursive helper.
parts.tests:
t = BST()
for x in [5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 7, 9]:
    t.insert(x)
assert t.inorder() == [1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9], 'in-order traversal of a BST gives sorted order'
assert BST().inorder() == [], 'an empty tree gives an empty list'

title: Implement a hash table with probing
intro: A hash table stores each key in a slot computed by a hash function. When that home slot is taken (a collision), probing tries further slots in a fixed sequence. Build it part by part: hashing and insert with linear probing, search, then a quadratic-probing subclass. (Syllabus 1.2 / 2.3: hash table search.)

parts.instruction: Write the constructor __init__(capacity) with a list self._slots of capacity None values. Add _hash(key) = sum(ord(c) for c in key) % capacity, and _probe(key, i), which returns the slot to try on attempt i using LINEAR probing: (self._hash(key) + i) % self._capacity. Then add insert(key): probe i = 0, 1, 2, ... until you find an empty slot or the key itself (re-inserting a key does nothing), store the key and return True; return False if the table is full.
parts.tests:
h = HashTable(5)
assert h._hash('ab') == (97 + 98) % 5, 'hash sums character codes modulo capacity'
assert h.insert('a') == True and h.insert('f') == True, 'both inserts succeed'
assert h._slots[2] == 'a' and h._slots[3] == 'f', 'a collides (97 and 102 both hash to 2), so f probes one slot on'
assert h.insert('a') == True and h._slots.count('a') == 1, 're-inserting the same key stores it once'
h2 = HashTable(2)
h2.insert('a'); h2.insert('c')
assert h2.insert('e') == False, 'insert returns False when the table is full'

parts.instruction: Add search(key), which returns True if key is stored and False otherwise. Follow the SAME probe sequence as insert - start at the home slot and keep probing while slots are occupied, stopping at the first empty slot.
parts.tests:
h = HashTable(5)
h.insert('a'); h.insert('f'); h.insert('k')
assert h.search('a') == True and h.search('k') == True, 'search finds keys, including ones that collided (97, 102 and 107 all hash to 2)'
assert h.search('b') == False, 'a missing key returns False'
assert HashTable(5).search('a') == False, 'an empty table holds nothing'

parts.instruction: Now write a subclass QuadraticHashTable(HashTable) that overrides ONLY _probe(key, i) to use quadratic probing: (self._hash(key) + i * i) % self._capacity. insert and search from the parent then probe quadratically with no other changes, because they call self._probe.
parts.tests:
h = QuadraticHashTable(11)
h.insert('a'); h.insert('l'); h.insert('w')
assert h._slots[9] == 'a', 'a sits at its home slot (97 mod 11 = 9)'
assert h._slots[10] == 'l', 'l collides and moves 1 slot on'
assert h._slots[2] == 'w', 'w collides twice and lands at (9 + 2*2) mod 11 = 2, not the linear slot 0'
assert h.search('a') == True and h.search('l') == True and h.search('w') == True, 'search follows the same quadratic sequence'
assert h.search('z') == False, 'a missing key returns False'

title: Implement linear search
intro: Linear search checks every item in order until it finds the target or runs out of items - O(n) time. Part 1 is the basic search; part 2 counts the comparisons, which is how algorithm cost is measured. (Syllabus 1.2 / 2.3: linear search.)

parts.instruction: Write linear_search(items, target), which returns the index of the FIRST occurrence of target in items, or -1 if target is not in the list. Do not use list.index() - write the loop.
parts.tests:
assert linear_search([5, 3, 8, 1], 8) == 2, 'return the index of the target'
assert linear_search([5, 3, 8, 1], 5) == 0 and linear_search([5, 3, 8, 1], 1) == 3, 'first and last positions work'
assert linear_search([5, 3, 8, 1], 9) == -1, 'missing target gives -1'
assert linear_search([], 9) == -1, 'an empty list gives -1'
assert linear_search([2, 2, 2], 2) == 0, 'return the FIRST occurrence'

parts.instruction: Write linear_search_count(items, target), which works like linear_search but returns a tuple (index, comparisons), where comparisons is how many item-to-target comparisons were made. A missing target in a 4-item list takes 4 comparisons.
parts.tests:
assert linear_search_count([5, 3, 8, 1], 8) == (2, 3), 'finding the 3rd item takes 3 comparisons'
assert linear_search_count([5, 3, 8, 1], 5) == (0, 1), 'first item takes 1 comparison'
assert linear_search_count([5, 3, 8, 1], 9) == (-1, 4), 'a missing target checks all 4 items'
assert linear_search_count([], 9) == (-1, 0), 'an empty list takes 0 comparisons'

title: Implement binary search
intro: Binary search halves a SORTED list each step: check the middle, then keep only the half that can hold the target - O(log n) time. Part 1 is the iterative search; part 2 counts comparisons to show the halving. (Syllabus 1.2 / 2.3: binary search.)

parts.instruction: Write binary_search(items, target), which returns the index of target in the SORTED list items, or -1 if it is not there. Keep low and high indexes, look at the middle, and discard half the list each step. Do not use a plain loop over every item.
parts.tests:
assert binary_search([1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9], 5) == 3, 'return the index of the target'
assert binary_search([1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9], 1) == 0 and binary_search([1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9], 9) == 6, 'both ends work'
assert binary_search([1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9], 6) == -1, 'missing target gives -1'
assert binary_search([], 1) == -1 and binary_search([4], 4) == 0, 'empty and single-item lists work'

parts.instruction: Write binary_search_count(items, target), which works like binary_search but returns (index, comparisons). Halving means 1000 sorted items need at most 11 comparisons - that is O(log n) in practice.
parts.tests:
big = sorted(range(0, 2000, 2))
idx, comps = binary_search_count(big, 1998)
assert big[idx] == 1998 and comps <= 11, '1000 items take at most 11 comparisons'
idx, comps = binary_search_count(big, 999)
assert idx == -1 and comps <= 11, 'a missing target is ruled out just as fast'
assert binary_search_count([1, 3, 5], 3) == (1, 1), 'a lucky first guess takes 1 comparison'

title: Implement bubble sort
intro: Bubble sort passes through the list swapping neighbours that are out of order, so the largest unsorted item bubbles to the end each pass - O(n^2) time. Part 1 is the basic sort; part 2 adds the early-exit optimisation. (Syllabus 1.2 / 2.3: bubble sort.)

parts.instruction: Write bubble_sort(items), which returns a NEW sorted list and leaves the original unchanged. Compare neighbours and swap when they are out of order; after each pass the largest unsorted item is in place, so each pass can stop one item earlier.
parts.tests:
assert bubble_sort([5, 1, 4, 2]) == [1, 2, 4, 5], 'sorts the list'
orig = [5, 1, 4, 2]
bubble_sort(orig)
assert orig == [5, 1, 4, 2], 'the original list is unchanged'
assert bubble_sort([1, 2, 3]) == [1, 2, 3] and bubble_sort([3, 2, 1]) == [1, 2, 3], 'sorted and reversed lists work'
assert bubble_sort([]) == [] and bubble_sort([2, 2, 1]) == [1, 2, 2], 'empty and duplicate lists work'

parts.instruction: Write bubble_sort_passes(items), which returns (sorted_list, passes). If a pass makes NO swaps the list is already sorted, so stop early. passes counts every pass, including the final no-swap pass - so a reversed 4-item list takes 3 working passes and a nearly sorted one takes 2.
parts.tests:
assert bubble_sort_passes([4, 3, 2, 1]) == ([1, 2, 3, 4], 3), 'a reversed list needs n-1 working passes (every pass swaps, so no early exit)'
assert bubble_sort_passes([1, 2, 3, 5, 4]) == ([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2), 'one fix pass plus one no-swap pass'
assert bubble_sort_passes([1, 2, 3]) == ([1, 2, 3], 1), 'already sorted: a single no-swap pass'
assert bubble_sort_passes([]) == ([], 0), 'an empty list needs no passes'

title: Implement insertion sort
intro: Insertion sort grows a sorted left-hand side: take the next item and shift it left into its correct place, like sorting a hand of cards - O(n^2) time, but fast on nearly sorted data. (Syllabus 1.2 / 2.3: insertion sort.)

parts.instruction: Write insertion_sort(items), which returns a NEW sorted list and leaves the original unchanged. For each item from the second onward, shift it left past every larger item until it sits in the right place.
parts.tests:
assert insertion_sort([5, 1, 4, 2]) == [1, 2, 4, 5], 'sorts the list'
orig = [5, 1, 4, 2]
insertion_sort(orig)
assert orig == [5, 1, 4, 2], 'the original list is unchanged'
assert insertion_sort([1, 2, 3]) == [1, 2, 3] and insertion_sort([3, 2, 1]) == [1, 2, 3], 'sorted and reversed lists work'
assert insertion_sort([]) == [] and insertion_sort([2, 2, 1]) == [1, 2, 2], 'empty and duplicate lists work'

parts.instruction: Write insertion_sort_shifts(items), which returns (sorted_list, shifts), where shifts counts how many times an item moves one position left. A reversed 3-item list takes 3 shifts (2 + 1 = n(n-1)/2); a sorted list takes 0 - that is why insertion sort suits nearly sorted data.
parts.tests:
assert insertion_sort_shifts([3, 2, 1]) == ([1, 2, 3], 3), 'reversed: 2 + 1 = 3 shifts'
assert insertion_sort_shifts([1, 2, 3]) == ([1, 2, 3], 0), 'already sorted: no shifts'
assert insertion_sort_shifts([2, 1, 3]) == ([1, 2, 3], 1), 'one item one place left'
assert insertion_sort_shifts([]) == ([], 0), 'empty list'

title: Implement merge sort
intro: Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves - O(n log n) time. Part 1 is merge, the heart of the algorithm; part 2 is the recursive sort. (Syllabus 1.2 / 2.3: merge sort.)

parts.instruction: Write merge(left, right), which takes two SORTED lists and returns one sorted list containing all their items. Walk both lists with two indexes, always taking the smaller front item. Do not just concatenate and sort.
parts.tests:
assert merge([1, 4, 5], [2, 3]) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'merges two sorted lists'
assert merge([], [1, 2]) == [1, 2] and merge([1, 2], []) == [1, 2], 'one side can be empty'
assert merge([1, 3], [1, 3]) == [1, 1, 3, 3], 'duplicates from both sides survive'
assert merge([2], [1]) == [1, 2], 'single items work'

parts.instruction: Write merge_sort(items), which returns a NEW sorted list: if the list has fewer than 2 items return a copy; otherwise split it in half, merge_sort each half, and merge the results.
parts.tests:
assert merge_sort([5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 0]) == [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 8], 'sorts the list'
orig = [3, 1, 2]
merge_sort(orig)
assert orig == [3, 1, 2], 'the original list is unchanged'
assert merge_sort([]) == [] and merge_sort([7]) == [7], 'empty and single-item lists work'
assert merge_sort([2, 2, 1]) == [1, 2, 2], 'duplicates work'

title: Implement quicksort
intro: Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the list so smaller items sit left of the pivot and larger items right, then sorts each side recursively - O(n log n) on average. Part 1 is the in-place partition; part 2 is the recursive sort. (Syllabus 1.2 / 2.3: quicksort.)

parts.instruction: Write partition(items, low, high), which takes the LAST item in the range as the pivot, rearranges items IN PLACE so everything before the pivot's final position is <= pivot and everything after is > pivot, and returns the pivot's final index. Walk the range swapping items <= pivot toward the front, then swap the pivot into place.
parts.starter:
def partition(items, low, high):
    # pivot = items[high]; move items <= pivot to the front of the range
    # then swap the pivot into its final spot and return that index
    pass
parts.tests:
a = [3, 1, 5, 2, 4]
p = partition(a, 0, 4)
assert p == 3 and a == [3, 1, 2, 4, 5], 'pivot 4 lands at index 3 with smaller items to its left'
assert all(x <= a[p] for x in a[:p]) and all(x > a[p] for x in a[p+1:]), 'the partition property holds'
b = [2, 1]
p = partition(b, 0, 1)
assert p == 0 and b == [1, 2], 'a two-item range works: pivot 1 lands at index 0'

parts.instruction: Write quick_sort(items), which sorts the list IN PLACE using partition: recursively sort the ranges left and right of the pivot's final position, then return items. (A helper _quick_sort(items, low, high) keeps the public call simple.)
parts.tests:
a = [5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 0]
assert quick_sort(a) == [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 8] and a == [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 8], 'sorts in place and returns the list'
assert quick_sort([]) == [] and quick_sort([7]) == [7], 'empty and single-item lists work'
assert quick_sort([2, 2, 1]) == [1, 2, 2], 'duplicates work'
